title: Congenital melanocytic naevi (CMN)
summary: Moles present at birth. Melanoma risk depends on size: small and medium CMN carry a low (<1%) lifetime risk, large and giant ones about 2–5%, higher with many satellites. Lifelong surveillance and support matter more than surgery.

glance.think: A child with a brown or black, often hairy birthmark mole, sometimes large with smaller satellite moles.
glance.engine: Post-zygotic NRAS mutation in melanocyte precursors; earlier mutation means a larger naevus and more satellites.
glance.backbone: Classify by projected adult size; refer large/giant or multiple CMN to paediatric dermatology; MRI in infants with 2 or more CMN at birth; teach families what change to report.
glance.never_miss: Melanoma in large/giant CMN (often deep or in childhood); neurocutaneous melanosis; psychological impact.

what: A melanocytic naevus present at birth (or appearing in the first year, "tardive"). About 1% of newborns have one; large/giant ones occur in about 1 in 20,000.
cause: **Post-zygotic NRAS mutation** in neural-crest melanoblasts (BRAF in some small CMN). The earlier the mutation, the larger the naevus and the more likely satellites and neurocutaneous melanosis (CNS melanocytes).

list: **Size by projected adult size (PAS)**: small <1.5 cm; medium 1.5–20 cm (M1 1.5–10 cm, M2 10–20 cm); **large 20–40 cm**; **giant >40 cm**

Head lesions roughly double, and trunk and limb lesions roughly triple, from infancy to adulthood. **A 30 cm trunk CMN at age 5 projects to >40 cm, so it is a giant CMN** ([Case 2](condition:melanocytic-naevi).

Features: brown to black, often hairy, with varied texture. **They become rougher, lumpy, hairier or lighter with time**. These are benign maturation changes (the course point), but a new **firm nodule, ulceration, rapid growth or pain** needs urgent assessment. Also proliferative nodules (benign) occur in infancy.
**Satellite naevi** and **multiple CMN** (≥2 at birth) are markers for **neurocutaneous melanosis/CNS involvement** (seizures, developmental delay, hydrocephalus).

diagnosis: Clinical, with serial photographs. Biopsy of new nodules. **MRI of brain and spine** (ideally in the first 6 months of life, before myelination, under natural sleep) in children with **≥2 CMN at birth, of any size** (the current UK expert approach; Kinsler). It is not routine for a single CMN without neurological signs.
differentials: Café-au-lait macule (flat, no hair, uniform), Becker naevus (acquired, adolescent shoulder, hairy), dermal melanocytosis ("Mongolian spot", blue-grey, sacral), speckled lentiginous naevus (naevus spilus), smooth muscle hamartoma, and plexiform neurofibroma with overlying pigment.

list: **Melanoma risk by size (corrected; related question):** **Small and medium CMN: lifetime melanoma risk is low (<1%)**, similar to or slightly above the general population, and melanoma usually arises after puberty at the junctional edge; **Large/giant CMN: around 2–5% overall (up to 10–15% in the highest-risk group: >40 cm PAS with many satellites/multiple CMN)**. Melanoma often arises in childhood and **deep** in the naevus or in the CNS, which is why surface excision does not remove the risk; The course "5–10%" belongs to the large/giant group, **not** to small/medium CMN
**Refer** (routine to paediatric dermatology; urgent for any new nodule, ulcer or rapid change) for **lifelong surveillance** and MDT input (dermatology, plastics, neurology, psychology).

**Prophylactic excision:** no evidence that it reduces melanoma risk in large/giant CMN (the course point). Surgery is for function, cosmesis or symptoms, as an MDT decision. **Laser** lightens the surface but leaves deep naevus cells and can make surveillance harder. It is not recommended routinely (specialist only).
**Support:** itch (emollients; antihistamines at night if needed); dry, fragile skin; psychological impact and bullying. Point families to *Caring Matters Now* (UK charity for CMN).
Sun protection, and **teach parents what change to report**.

red_flags: A new firm nodule, ulceration, rapid growth or pain within a CMN: **urgent** referral.
Two or more CMN at birth, or a large/giant CMN with satellites: refer for MRI and specialist surveillance.
pearls: The rough, hairy, raised changes the parent describes are expected. A **hard lump** is not.
If scalp CMN or multiple CMN plus headaches, vomiting or seizures, arrange **same-day** paediatric review.
